niche.title: How to Build an AH-64 Apache, One Problem at a Time
niche.description:
The AH-64 Apache is a twin-engine attack helicopter with a four-blade main rotor, now built by Boeing.
Bell's AH-1 Cobra, first flown in 1965, put its co-pilot/gunner in front of the pilot. The tandem seats made it narrow and hard to hit. The Apache uses the same layout: the co-pilot/gunner in front, the pilot in the rear.
The crew members sit in armored seats on an armor-plated floor. FAS says the Apache's critical areas can withstand hits from rounds up to 23 mm.
The crew seats and landing gear are designed to collapse slowly in a heavy landing, absorbing the impact energy.

niche.title: This Apache Has Two Seats. That Night It Carried Three Men
niche.description:
Iraq, 2007. A badly wounded soldier had waited more than 40 minutes for a medevac. Apache pilots Kevin Purtee and Allen Crist landed beside him; Crist gave the soldier his seat and rode outside on the stub wing, strapped to the airframe, for the few minutes to the medical pad. The next day the soldier wrote them a note, thanking them and apologizing for damaging their helicopter.

Sources: National Guard, nationalguard.mil/News/Article/573012; Whiteman AFB, "On a wing and a prayer".
3D animation by Aerospace Universe; cockpit cutaways are schematic.

niche.title: The First Shots of Desert Storm Came From Helicopters
niche.description:
The first shots of Desert Storm weren't fired by jets.

17 January 1991: eight AH-64 Apaches of Task Force Normandy flew 50 feet above the desert in total darkness. Their job: destroy two Iraqi early-warning radar sites at the same moment, because if either survived it could raise the alarm. Air Force MH-53J Pave Low helicopters led the way using GPS and terrain-following radar, dropping chemlights to mark the final checkpoint. niche.title: How Apache Pilots See at Night (IHADSS Explained by a Former Pilot)
niche.description:
How do Apache pilots see at night? A former AH-64 Apache and AH-6 Little Bird pilot explains the IHADSS, the monocle Apache pilots wear over their right eye.

The PNVS (Pilot Night Vision Sensor) is a forward-looking infrared camera on the nose of the Apache, mounted above the TADS. It's slaved to your helmet, so it turns wherever you turn your head, and its thermal image is projected in front of your right eye with your flight symbology on top. At night, you're flying off that one eye. In this video I break down:

 • The tandem cockpit, TADS and PNVS
